procedural_history.originating_court: Multiple courts across the country where FIRs were registered against the petitioners.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be the continued detention of Petitioner Nos. 1 and 2, and the potential for further arrests of Petitioner No. 3.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Chhattisgarh High Court granted bail to Petitioner No. 3 on 10.04.2023 in MCRC No. 724 / 2023.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached via a Writ Petition (Crl) No. 546 of 2023 under Article 32 of the Constitution, seeking directions to liquidate attached assets to expedite the release of Petitioners 1 and 2, who have been in jail for over 8 years. The Supreme Court also addressed concerns regarding the potential re-arrest of Petitioner No. 3, issuing orders to prevent his arrest in fresh cases on the same or related issues. Ultimately, the Supreme Court issued directions for the constitution of a High-Powered Sale Committee (HPSC) to auction the immovable assets of the companies involved.

issue.issue_text: Whether the facts of the case necessitated constitution of a High Powered Sale Committee, under Article 142 of the Constitution, to auction the immovable assets of the companies to satisfy the investors’ claims and liquidate all other statutory liabilities of the Companies.

facts: The promoters/directors of the companies had been in jail as undertrials for over 8 years.
Innocent investors had been waiting for a refund of their money for more than a decade.
The companies' immovable properties were spread across different parts of the country, making liquidation complex and difficult for a single body like SEBI or the MPID Court.
SEBI, despite its bona fide efforts, was facing an "uphill task" in conducting public auctions for all the assets.
The counsel for the parties, including the petitioners and SEBI, mutually suggested and agreed to the formation of a High-Powered Sale Committee (HPSC).
law: Article 142 of the Constitution of India grants the Supreme Court the power to pass any decree or make any order necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it.
application: The Court recognized that it was practically "unachievable" for either SEBI or the MPID Court to liquidate all the geographically dispersed assets in a time-bound manner due to the complexity of the process.
Considering the significant delay, with promoters in jail for over 8 years and investors awaiting refunds for over a decade, the Court found it necessary to expedite the process.
Since all parties, including SEBI, fairly agreed to the proposal, the Court saw the constitution of an HPSC as a viable and efficient solution.
The Court invoked its extraordinary powers under Article 142 to create the HPSC, chaired by a former Supreme Court judge, to ensure complete justice for the investors.
To make the committee effective, the Court vested it with all the powers of a Civil Court to enable it to take all necessary actions to speed up the liquidation of the properties.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the proposal and decided to constitute a High-Powered Sale Committee under Article 142 of the Constitution. This decision was based on the practical difficulties faced by SEBI, the extensive delay in refunding investors, the consensus among the parties, and the need to ensure a speedy and just resolution by liquidating the companies' assets to pay off investors and other liabilities.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the facts of the case necessitated constitution of a High Powered Sale Committee, under Article 142 of the Constitution, to auction the immovable assets of the companies to satisfy the investors’ claims and liquidate all other statutory liabilities of the Companies.
appellant_arguments: The petitioners argued for the liquidation of the attached assets of their companies to repay investors.
They requested the court to direct Respondent No. 1 to liquidate the assets within six months.
In the alternative, they asked to be allowed to assist Respondent No. 1 in the liquidation process and in identifying genuine investors.
respondent_arguments: The text does not indicate that the respondents opposed the formation of a committee. Instead, it states that the court considered "valuable suggestions given by learned Senior Counsel/Counsel for the parties for the constitution of HPSC," implying that the respondents participated in and likely consented to this course of action.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Article 142 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has the authority to constitute a High Powered Sale Committee to auction the immovable assets of companies in order to satisfy investors’ claims and liquidate other statutory liabilities when the facts of the case necessitate such an action.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the existing statutory bodies, namely SEBI and the MPID Court, were not equipped with the necessary infrastructure or strategic capabilities to manage the complex and large-scale task of identifying, valuing, and auctioning the companies' properties to secure their true market value in a timely manner. This institutional inadequacy, coupled with the indefinite timeline for the conclusion of pending criminal trials and the potential for prejudice to all parties from further delays, necessitated the formation of a High Powered Sale Committee under Article 142 to ensure an efficient and fair liquidation of assets for the benefit of the investors.
legal_tests_applied: The court exercised its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution, which is invoked to do 'complete justice' in cases where existing statutory mechanisms are found to be insufficient or inadequate to address the specific facts and circumstances. The test for its application was met by the finding that neither SEBI nor the MPID Court could effectively and promptly liquidate the assets to repay investors.
policy_considerations: The court recognized that specialized bodies like SEBI or the MPID Court do not have the 'readily available infrastructural and strategical facilities' to conduct a large-scale property auction, including identifying each property, assessing its fair market value, and auctioning it to fetch its true value.

Relying on the standard legal process was deemed unviable because 'The conclusion of trials in the pending criminal cases is marred by uncertainty,' which would indefinitely delay resolution for the investors.
The court acted to prevent harm to all stakeholders, noting that 'any further delay in this regard, will be prejudicial to one and all.'

The court considered the petitioners' stated intent to repay investors, noting that 'The Petitioners have shown their bona fide towards refunding the investors’ amounts,' which supported a proactive solution over waiting for the conclusion of adversarial proceedings.
